text: So will Mamdani's rent freeze fix New York housing? No. Will it help some people? Yes. And that is exactly why this debate is more complicated than both sides want it to be. By the way, this is a second video about NYC housing situation and Mamdani's rent freeze. Please watch part one if you didn't. If you are a rent-stabilized tenant and your renewal increase is zero, that is not fake. That is real money. In a city where rent is insane and vacancy is around 1.4%, a rent freeze can mean a breathing room. It can mean not being forced out of your neighborhood. It can mean stability for families, older tenants, immigrants, lower-income workers, and people who simply cannot absorb another hike. So I understand why some people support it. But here's the problem. A rent freeze is not a housing policy cure. It is a painkiller. It treats the pain of some current tenants, but it doesn't fix the reason the pain exists in the first place. Too many people fighting over too few homes. And this is the insider-outsider problem. If you already have a rent-stabilized apartment, congratulations, you are inside a castle. Your rent increase is limited, you have stronger renewal rights, and now, under Mamdani's rent freeze, your rent doesn't go up for the covered period. But if you do not have a rent-stabilized apartment, you are outside the castle, fighting in the market rate jungle with everyone else. And the jungle is not kind. This is one of the big problems with rent control in general. It protects current tenants, but it also makes the housing market more rigid. People hold on to apartments longer, even when the apartment no longer fits their needs. A single person may stay in a large stabilized apartment because leaving would mean entering the market rate nightmare. A family that actually needs that space cannot get it. Again, the tenant is not evil. The tenant is responding rationally to a broken system. Then there's the landlord side. Some people talk about landlords as if every landlord is a cartoon billionaire smoking a cigar on a pile of rent checks. And yes, many rent-stabilized apartments are controlled by large ownership portfolios. The tiny mom-and-pop landlord is often exaggerated in political debates. But smaller landlords do exist. Older, fully rent-stabilized buildings do exist. And some of them have much thinner margins than people assume. Because taxes do not freeze. Insurance does not freeze. Repairs do not freeze. Fuel, labor, maintenance, none of that freezes. So if rent is frozen at 0%, but costs keep rising, the remaining margin gets squeezed. Does that mean every landlord goes bankrupt? No, that would be ridiculous. But does it mean some weaker buildings may delay repairs, reduce maintenance, or become financially stressed? Yes, that risk is real. And this is one of the annoying things about housing policy. Sometimes tenants can win on paper and still lose in practice. The rent stays low, but the building gets worse. The elevator breaks. Repairs take longer. The hallway starts smelling like 1974. Congratulations, your rent is affordable, and so is the mold. So the real problem is not simply rent control. The real problem is severe shortage plus strict rules plus below-market apartments plus slow construction. That combination creates insiders and outsiders. Now, to be fair to Mamdani, he does seem to understand that supply matters. His block-by-block initiative talks about several actions against the housing problem, including building 200,000 new affordable housing units over the next 10 years. But if I'm being honest, you have to be very ambitious to believe this will seriously fix the problem. NYC already faces huge projected budget gaps. Mamdani's current term only runs until the end of 2029, while the housing plan runs for 10 years. Even if he wins re-election, that only takes him through 2033. And the plan still depends on future budgets, future councils, and future political conditions. Previous mayors like Bloomberg and de Blasio also had big affordable housing programs. And yet, after all of that, New York still ended up with one of the worst housing shortages in the country. And even if Mamdani does everything he promised, 200,000 new units over 10 years means around 20,000 units per year. That is not nothing, but for a city like New York, that is nowhere near enough. So overall, my conclusion is slightly different from both sides. I do not think Mamdani's rent freeze is as catastrophic as some critics say. New York's housing market is already so broken that one rent freeze is probably not going to single-handedly destroy it. But I also do not think it is as useful as supporters pretend. It helps some tenants, sure, especially people already inside the rent-stabilized system. But it doesn't solve the shortage. It leaves outsiders facing even more competition in the already brutal market. And it puts pressure on landlords, especially weaker and smaller ones. Because taxes, insurance, repairs, fuel, labor, and maintenance do not freeze just because rent does. The real solution is boring but politically painful. Build much more housing, deregulate construction where the rules only create delays, remove zoning limits that artificially restrict supply, allow more density, legalize more apartments, speed up permits from years to months, and stop pretending that you can fix a shortage by controlling prices.
